## What Is an Employer of Record in the Bahamas


An Employer of Record (EOR) is a third-party company that legally hires workers on behalf of another business. In the Bahamas, the EOR becomes the official employer for your Bahamian team members, handling payroll, tax withholdings, statutory benefits, and compliance with local labor law, while you retain full control over day-to-day work and responsibilities.


The Bahamas operates under the Employment Act, which governs working hours, leave entitlements, termination procedures, and employee protections. Without a registered legal entity in the country, you cannot hire locally in a compliant way. An EOR solves this by acting as the legal employer on the ground, so you can[hire globally without the complexity](https://www.bolto.com/global-hr) of setting up a subsidiary.


Here’s how the relationship works in practice:


- You select the candidate and define the role, compensation, and scope of work.
- The EOR signs the employment contract with the worker under Bahamian law and registers them with the relevant authorities.
- The EOR runs payroll, withholds National Insurance Board (NIB) contributions, and handles all statutory filings.
- You manage the worker's output and direction as you would any team member.


This structure is well-suited for companies testing the Bahamian market, hiring a single specialist, or scaling a distributed team without the time and cost of local entity formation.


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in the Bahamas


The Bahamas operates under a well-defined legal framework for employment, and understanding it before you hire is worth your time. The primary governing legislation is the[Employment Act](http://www.departmentoflabour.gov.bs/department-of-labour-laws-online) , which sets out the baseline rights and obligations for employers and employees across the country.


Here are the key compliance requirements you need to know:


- The standard workweek is 40 hours, and any hours beyond that generally qualify for overtime pay, though the exact rate can depend on the role and agreement in place, so check current terms under the[Employment Act](http://www.departmentoflabour.gov.bs/department-of-labour-laws-online) .
- Employees are typically entitled to a minimum of two weeks of paid annual leave after completing one year of continuous service.
- Under the Bahamas Employment Act, employers are generally required to provide paid sick leave, though the specific terms can vary by employment contract and length of service.
- Employers and employees both contribute to the[National Insurance Board (NIB)](https://www.nib-bahamas.com/) , which funds social security benefits including retirement, disability, and sickness coverage. Contribution rates apply to both parties and are calculated as a percentage of insurable wages.
- Maternity leave protections are in place under the Employment Act, with qualifying employees generally entitled to paid leave around childbirth.
- Under the Employment Act, termination generally requires prescribed notice periods based on length of service, and employees terminated without cause may be entitled to severance pay.


Staying on top of these obligations is where many growing businesses run into trouble, particularly when managing payroll contributions to the NIB and keeping employment contracts aligned with local law. An Employer of Record (EOR) handles these filings and agreements on your behalf, so you are not left piecing together compliance requirements from scratch.


This is general information, not legal advice. Rules vary by situation and change over time, so consult a qualified employment lawyer for your specific circumstances.

## EOR vs. Local Entity in the Bahamas: Which Is Right for You


When you want to hire someone in the Bahamas, you have two main paths: set up a local legal entity or work through an Employer of Record (EOR). Here’s how to think through the choice.


Setting up a local entity gives you full direct control and can make sense if you’re building a large, permanent team in the country, though for many the[best EOR for startups](https://www.bolto.com/blog/what-is-the-best-eor-for-startups) is the smarter starting point. The tradeoff is time and cost. Entity formation in the Bahamas typically takes several months, requires ongoing accounting and legal maintenance, and demands familiarity with local corporate law before you can hire a single person.


An EOR lets you skip that process entirely. The EOR becomes the legal employer on paper, handling payroll, tax filings, and compliance with Bahamian labor law while your hire works for you day-to-day.


### When an EOR Makes More Sense


- You're hiring one to a few people and a full entity would cost more to maintain than it saves.
- You want to move quickly and can't wait months for entity setup to clear.
- You're testing the Bahamas as a market before committing to a permanent local presence.
- You want someone else managing compliance as local labor rules change.

- Your business model requires a registered local presence for licensing or regulatory reasons specific to your industry.
- You have legal and HR resources in-house to manage local obligations directly.


For most companies hiring their first few team members in the Bahamas, reviewing the[best global EOR providers for startups](https://www.bolto.com/blog/best-global-eor-providers-for-startups) is the faster and lower-risk starting point. Entity setup becomes worth considering once your local team grows large enough that the economics shift in its favor.
